text: And I, brothers, could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as people of the flesh, as infants in Christ.
I gave you milk to drink, not solid food, for you were not yet ready for it. And even now you are not ready,
for you are still worldly. For where there is jealousy and quarreling among you, are you not worldly, living like mere human beings?

versions.text: for you are still worldly. As long as there is jealousy and quarreling among you, are you not worldly, living like mere human beings?
versions.explanation: The Greek ὅπου γὰρ is locative-causal ("for where..."), not temporal ("as long as"). "As long as" introduces a condition of duration that the Greek does not express, and it also drops the connective γάρ that links the clause to the preceding statement.

text: For when one says, "I follow Paul," and another, "I follow Apollos," are you not merely human?
What, then, is Apollos? What is Paul? Servants through whom you came to believe, each as the Lord assigned him.
I planted, Apollos watered, but God made it grow.
So neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but only God, who makes it grow.
The one who plants and the one who waters are one, and each will receive his own reward according to his own labor.
For we are God's fellow workers; you are God's field, God's building.
By the grace of God given to me, like a skilled master builder I laid a foundation, and someone else is building on it. But let each one be careful how he builds,

versions.text: By the grace of God given to me, I laid the foundation like a skilled master builder, and someone else is building on it. But let each one be careful how he builds,
versions.explanation: θεμέλιον is anarthrous here ("a foundation"); the definite "the foundation" anticipates v. 11 prematurely. Placing the simile before the verb also follows the Greek order and reads more smoothly aloud.

text: for no one can lay any foundation other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ.
If anyone builds on this foundation with gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, or straw,
the work of each will be made plain, for the Day will bring it to light. It will be revealed with fire, and the fire will test the quality of each one's work.
If anyone's work that he has built on it survives, he will receive a reward.

versions.text: If what someone has built survives, he will receive a reward.
versions.explanation: The Greek keeps "work" (τὸ ἔργον) as the subject, matching the parallel in v. 13 and v. 15 where "work" is retained. The present rendering flattens the parallelism and omits the sense of building "on it" (ἐποικοδόμησεν).

text: If someone's work is burned up, he will suffer loss; he himself will be saved, but only as one escaping through the flames.
Do you not know that you are God's temple and that God's Spirit dwells in you?
If anyone destroys God's temple, God will destroy him. For God's temple is holy, and that temple is you.
Let no one deceive himself. If any of you thinks he is wise in this age, let him become a fool, so that he may become wise.
For the wisdom of this world is foolishness in God's sight. As it is written: "He catches the wise in their own craftiness."
And again: "The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are futile."
So let no one boast in men, for everything is yours:

versions.text: So let no one boast in human leaders, for everything is yours:
versions.explanation: ἐν ἀνθρώποις simply means "in men / in human beings"; "leaders" is an interpretive addition not present in the text, and it narrows Paul's broader point. Keeping "men" also preserves the link with κατὰ ἄνθρωπον / ἄνθρωποι in vv. 3–4.

text: whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas, whether the world or life or death, whether the present or the future—all is yours,
and you are Christ's, and Christ is God's.
